title: Halving cards in no order
hook: Binary search needs a sorted list. Except when the question is 'find a peak'.

knows: binary search halves a sorted list (binary-search)
doesNotKnow: that halving works on unsorted data for some questions

misconception: Halving only works on sorted lists.
objective: The learner can explain that comparing the middle card with its right neighbour shows which half is uphill, that walking uphill must reach a peak inside that half, so the other half can be discarded unseen; on 7 cards this never needs more than 5 turns.

claims.text: On the stage's cards (2 5 1 4 7 3 6, face down), the rule turns 4 of the 7 cards and ends on 6, which is a peak even though 7 is bigger.
claims.source: Builder's node run of the rule: compare positions 4 and 5 (4 < 7, go right), then 6 and 7 (3 < 6, go right), stop at position 7: value 6, neighbour 3. The order was written for the lesson to show a peak that is not the maximum. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own node run on 2 5 1 4 7 3 6: compares (4,7), (3,6); turns 4 cards; ends on 6 (neighbour 3).

claims.text: A peak only has to be not smaller than its neighbours.
claims.source: Definition used in the lesson's question and in MIT 6.006 (Demaine and Devadas, 2011), lecture 1, peak finding. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): MIT 6.006 Fall 2011 lecture 1 (Demaine, Devadas): b is a peak iff b >= a and b >= c. Stage reveal says 'only has to beat its neighbours'; with distinct cards this is the same, but 'not be smaller than' would match c2 exactly (non-blocking).

claims.text: If the right card is bigger, walking uphill to the right must reach a peak before the edge, so the left half can go unseen.
claims.source: Walk right from position m + 1 while the next card is bigger; the walk stops at a card not smaller than its right neighbour (or at the end), and its left neighbour is smaller by construction, so it is a peak in the kept half. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Re-derived with the invariant H[lo-1] < H[lo] and H[hi] > H[hi+1]; walk stays in the kept half.

claims.text: Over all 5,040 orders of 7 cards the rule always finds a peak and never needs more than 5 turns, about 2 per halving.
claims.source: Builder's exhaustive node check over all 7! orders of 1..7: always a peak; 4 turns in 3,780 orders, 5 in 1,260. Logarithmic bound: MIT 6.006 (2011) lecture 1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own exhaustive check over all 5,040 permutations: always a peak; 4 turns 3,780, 5 turns 1,260.

recall.question: In a list in no order, the middle number is 40 and its right neighbour is 55. Where must there be a peak (a number not smaller than its neighbours)?
options: In the right half, from 55 onward
Nowhere can be sure without sorting
recall.why: Walking uphill from 55 to the right must stop at a peak before or at the end, so the right half holds one. The left half may too, but you do not need it.
